title: Verifiable immunization records across borders: the policy-maker track
description: The seven modules (M1 to M7) of the DPI-H workshop's policy-maker track, taught from the journeys J1 to J4.1 of one cross-border family: domestic and cross-border verifiable immunization records as the entry point to a personal health record.
audience: Ministry of Health policy makers and digital health leads, at tables of one country each
promise: You will not leave with an assessment or a plan. You will leave knowing what each consists of, where your country stands on its first page, and who you would do the rest with.
useCaseStatement: A child vaccinated in ___ should be able to ___ in ___.

modules.title: From journey to capabilities
modules.carries: What had to exist for this moment to work — and where does our version of the journey break?
objectives: Name the capabilities each moment of the journey needs
Say where your country's version of the journey breaks
Choose a substitution pattern that gets you moving

modules.title: The reference architecture and where you stand

modules.title: Standards, specifications and the core data set
modules.carries: Which standards do we adopt rather than author — and who owns the national core data set?

modules.title: Trust, credentials and wallets
modules.carries: Who signs, who verifies, and who would hold the national trust anchor? Name it; do not decide it.

modules.title: Governance, decision rights and the legal basis
modules.carries: Who holds each decision — and what legal basis lets the record cross a border and be shared for a child?
objectives: Name who holds each of the four decision rights today

modules.title: Doing it together
modules.carries: Would your neighbour need this too? If yes, why would you each build it?

modules.title: First move and the investment required
modules.carries: What is realistic in twelve months with the people and money we have — and who owns it?

Name the cost driver that dominates it

steps.askTheRoom: What is the minimum a family should leave hospital with when their baby has no national ID?
steps.facilitatorCue: Start with Khamla, not the technology. Hold up a paper card: this is the only thing that crosses the border.

questions.text: Write your country’s use-case statement: “A child vaccinated in ___ should be able to ___ in ___.”
Who in your government would sign this card on behalf of the health sector: the hospital, the ministry, or a national trust service?
Does your law let a facility issue a health credential to a child who is not a citizen and has no national ID?

capabilities.label: A national service that signs vaccination certificates
An immunization record at the birth facility

tags.why: Issue to the WHO digital certificate specification rather than design a national card.

steps.askTheRoom: Is an “unverified but recorded” vaccine useful to the next clinician — or a risk?
steps.facilitatorCue: This is the key trust boundary in the story. Pause and make sure everyone sees why the CHW does not verify.

questions.text: Does your national core data set tell a dose the family reported from one that was verified? Who defines that element?
Who is allowed to verify a foreign credential: a health worker’s phone, a clinic, or only a national service?

capabilities.label: A core data set that marks a dose as reported or verified

tags.why: Take the element from the WHO immunization core data dictionary rather than define it nationally.

steps.askTheRoom: Who should be allowed to create a health identity for a newborn — and how early?
steps.facilitatorCue: Ask who in the room has worked with CHWs. What does “offline” really mean in their context?

questions.text: Which block gives this child his first identifier in your country: birth registration, the national ID, or the health client registry? Exists, partial or absent?
When a birth happened abroad and is not registered at home, how does the child enter your registries — and your coverage denominator?
Who may create a health identity for a newborn at a home visit, and on whose consent?

capabilities.label: A client registry that can hold a child with no birth record
A link from birth registration (CRVS) to the health registries
An offline app for community health workers
A referral from the community to a facility

tags.why: One population first: newborns found in border districts.

steps.askTheRoom: When verification fails, what should the nurse do — and how is it explained to the family?
steps.facilitatorCue: Open screen S4 (See what Nurse Chanthason sees) and switch it from Valid card to Tampered card live. The contrast lands better than any explanation.

questions.text: What must be true for this nurse to trust a record she did not create?
Who would hold your national trust anchor, and who accepts a foreign signature on behalf of your health sector?
What must your country have, and what must it decide, before it can verify a neighbour’s card offline? Name it; do not decide it here.

capabilities.label: Membership of a trust network, its list cached for offline use

tags.why: The trust network is built once, for every programme that signs credentials, not for immunization alone.

steps.askTheRoom: Who should own the mapping between countries’ vaccine codes — WHO, each country, or each clinic?
steps.facilitatorCue: Emphasize: the Taifafeki record is never overwritten. Both codes live side by side.

questions.text: Who owns the national core data set and the mapping between other countries’ vaccine codes and yours?
Which code systems do you use for vaccine products, and is the licence question settled?
Would your neighbour need this mapping too? If yes, why would you each build it?

capabilities.label: A terminology service holding vaccine codes and mappings
The national schedule as computable decision logic

tags.why: Map to a shared regional or international code set rather than one country at a time.

steps.askTheRoom: How do we design for shared phones without compromising each person’s privacy?
steps.facilitatorCue: Notice Khamla’s mood dips here. Ask the room why — this is the equity tension in the story.

questions.text: Is a family wallet a national service, a private app, or both — and who decides which apps may hold a record?
Who may hold and share a child’s record: either parent, a guardian, the child from what age? What does your law say about dependants?

capabilities.label: A wallet or citizen app that holds a family’s records
Rules for a parent holding a child’s record

tags.why: One credential first: the child’s vaccination record, on the phone the family already has.

steps.askTheRoom: Is a 4-digit spoken passcode the right balance of security and ease for this family?
steps.facilitatorCue: Ask: what is inside this QR? (Answer: not the health data — just a pointer and a key.)

questions.text: What legal basis lets a record held at home be opened by a clinician abroad, on the family’s consent?
Would one clause in your procurement — conformance to the national IG — be enough for your portal to issue this link?
Who sets how a shared link is protected — the passcode, how long it lasts, who may open it: a national rule, or the family’s choice?
Should the part of the record that crosses borders (IPS plus an immunization core) be profiled once for the region, with national extensions left sovereign?

capabilities.label: A national health record the family’s link points to
A service that issues time-limited links on the family’s consent

tags.why: Adopt the IPS and an existing link specification rather than author a national format.

steps.askTheRoom: Should the family be notified every time their child’s record is viewed abroad?
steps.facilitatorCue: Close the loop: the story started and ends in Taifafeki. Ask what changed for each persona since step 1.

questions.text: What agreement makes every view abroad leave an entry in the home country’s log — and who reads it?
What would your country send to a regional connectathon within twelve months to prove this moment works?
What is a realistic twelve-month first move toward this moment, with a named owner — and which cost driver dominates it?

capabilities.label: A point-of-care viewer that accepts a foreign link
An access log kept in the home country

tags.why: Shared testing and one regional data model, rather than each pair of countries agreeing its own.

assessment.standingLine: “Absent” is a finding, not a failure — the question is only whether it blocks this use case.

discussion.question: How should national immunization systems handle temporary IDs for cross-border infants before civil registration is complete?
Why should offline CHW devices store foreign cards as “reported, not verified” rather than trying to verify them in the field?
When a monovalent vaccine is given abroad but the home schedule uses a combination (e.g. pentavalent), how should schedule rules calculate the doses still due?
What agreements do countries need so that a clinician viewing a record abroad triggers an audit entry back in the patient’s home country?

technical.label: Client registry and identifiers
technical.text: The same registry that gives Somsak a temporary id at home (J2b) is the one his IPS is assembled against (J4.0b). M2 asks whether it exists; M5 asks who may write to it.

technical.label: Signing and the trust list
technical.text: One PKI carries three moments: Taifafeki signs the DVCs (J1), Onesa verifies them offline (J3a), and Onesa's own key signs the VHL a Taifafeki viewer checks (J4.1). Built once, for every credential.

technical.label: Core data set and terminology
technical.text: The reported/verified element (J2a), the product code map (J3b) and the cross-border IPS profile (J4.0b) are one core data set, read at three points.

technical.label: Lifelong record and the share link
technical.text: The national record, the wallet and the gateway's audit log are one service seen from the family, the clinician and the ministry.

policy.label: Trust anchor (decision right)
policy.text: Who signs at home and who accepts a foreign signature is one decision; M4 names the holder, M5 asks under what mandate.

policy.label: Consent for dependants (legal basis)
policy.text: The child acts through his parents from birth to the clinic abroad; the same rule decides who registers him, who holds his record and who may share it.

policy.label: Cross-border legal basis
policy.text: Opening a home record abroad and logging the view at home need one agreement, which is cheaper to reach regionally than pair by pair.

policy.label: Core data set custody (decision right)
policy.text: Whoever owns the core data set owns the code maps to neighbours; the room decides whether that is a country, a region or WHO.

resources.description: The policy-maker track's glossary, each term linked to the DPI-H RA and DTH-PHC glossaries.

resources.title: Terms at J1
resources.body:
- **Electronic immunization registry (EIR)**: Records each person's doses. Often the first working part of a lifelong record.
- **Client Registry**: The Client Registry is the national authoritative source of health-specific person identity. It is the foundational health-sector component that maintains a unique, verifiable identity record for every person who accesses or is eligible to access health services within a jurisdiction.
- **Facility, workforce and product registries**: Authoritative lists of health facilities, health workers, and products such as vaccines and their batches.
- **Dose number and series**: Which dose this is, out of how many in the schedule. Needed to work out what is due next.
- **Batch number**: Identifies the production batch of a vaccine. Needed for recalls and safety checks.
- **Verifiable credential (VC)**: A digitally signed statement, such as a vaccination record, that anyone can check is genuine and unaltered.
- **Digital signature**: A cryptographic seal made with the issuer's private key. Verifiers check it with the matching public key.
- **Public key infrastructure (PKI)**: The keys, certificates and rules that make digital signatures trustworthy.
- **Issuer · holder · verifier**: The three roles: who signs the credential, who keeps it, and who checks it.
- **Health certificate identifier (HCID)**: The unique ID of an issued certificate.
- **International Certificate of Vaccination or Prophylaxis (ICVP)**: The "yellow card". The digital ICVP is its signed, verifiable form.
- **Consent**: A person's permission for their data to be used or shared. Rules for minors and dependants differ by country.

resources.title: Terms at J2a
resources.body:
- **Point-of-Service Applications**: Point-of-service applications are end-user application components (IT systems or software tools) used by individuals directly engaged in healthcare—such as clinicians, community health workers, and patients—that enable interaction with the broader healthcare ecosystem.
- **Verifiable credential (VC)**: A digitally signed statement, such as a vaccination record, that anyone can check is genuine and unaltered.
- **Digital signature**: A cryptographic seal made with the issuer's private key. Verifiers check it with the matching public key.
- **Core data set**: The elements a country agrees to record for a use case, each mapped to standard codes. Also called a minimum data set.

resources.title: Terms at J2b
resources.body:
- **Client Registry**: The Client Registry is the national authoritative source of health-specific person identity. It is the foundational health-sector component that maintains a unique, verifiable identity record for every person who accesses or is eligible to access health services within a jurisdiction.
- **Civil registration and vital statistics (CRVS)**: Birth registration can start a child's immunization record.
- **Point-of-Service Applications**: Point-of-service applications are end-user application components (IT systems or software tools) used by individuals directly engaged in healthcare—such as clinicians, community health workers, and patients—that enable interaction with the broader healthcare ecosystem.
- **Facility, workforce and product registries**: Authoritative lists of health facilities, health workers, and products such as vaccines and their batches.
- **Consent**: A person's permission for their data to be used or shared. Rules for minors and dependants differ by country.
- **Interoperability**: Interoperability is the standards-based capability of heterogeneous information systems to communicate, exchange data, and use the exchanged information to execute functions effectively.

resources.title: Terms at J3a
resources.body:
- **Trust list**: A published list of keys accepted as valid issuers. The GDHCN shares these between countries.
- **Global Digital Health Certification Network (GDHCN)**: WHO Global Digital Health Certification Network. A trust network so countries can verify each other's health documents. Countries onboard per use case.
- **Trust anchor**: The national authority whose key vouches for the health sector's signers.
- **Public key infrastructure (PKI)**: The keys, certificates and rules that make digital signatures trustworthy.
- **Digital signature**: A cryptographic seal made with the issuer's private key. Verifiers check it with the matching public key.
- **Issuer · holder · verifier**: The three roles: who signs the credential, who keeps it, and who checks it.
- **Verifiable credential (VC)**: A digitally signed statement, such as a vaccination record, that anyone can check is genuine and unaltered.

resources.title: Terms at J3b
resources.body:
- **Terminology Service**: The Terminology Service is a governed, publicly accessible service that manages, publishes, and provides access to the standardised terminologies, code systems, value sets, and concept maps used across the digital health ecosystem.
- **Core data set**: The elements a country agrees to record for a use case, each mapped to standard codes. Also called a minimum data set.
- **Logical information model**: The agreed structure of the data: elements, types and rules, independent of any software.
- **SNOMED CT**: Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine Clinical Terms is a structured clinical terminology standard for use in electronic health records.
- **Computable Decision Support Engine**: The Computable Decision Support Engine is a governed, shared application component that delivers context-appropriate, evidence-based guidance at the point of clinical decision-making by applying computable clinical rules and knowledge artefacts to person-specific health data.
- **SMART Guidelines**: Standards-based, Machine-readable, Adaptive, Requirements-based, Testable Guidelines are a comprehensive set of reusable digital health components (e.g., interoperability standards, code libraries, algorithms, technical and operational specifications) that transform the guideline adaptation and implementation process to preserve fidelity and accelerate uptake. SMART Guidelines provide a five-step pathway to advance the adoption of best clinical and data practices, even if a country is not yet fully digital.
- **Digital adaptation kit (DAK)**: Software-neutral L2 content: personas, workflows, core data dictionary, decision logic, indicators and requirements.
- **Dose number and series**: Which dose this is, out of how many in the schedule. Needed to work out what is due next.
- **Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI)**: The national immunization programme.

resources.title: Terms at J4.0a
resources.body:
- **Digital wallet**: An app where a person holds their credentials. A signed paper QR code can play the same role.
- **Personal health record (PHR)**: Health information the person can see and control, for example in a wallet or citizen app.
- **Lifelong Health Record**: The Lifelong Health Record (LHR) is one or more governed data repositories, whether physically consolidated or virtually federated, that collectively maintain a longitudinal, person-centred record of an individual's key health information across care settings and over their lifetime.
- **Consent**: A person's permission for their data to be used or shared. Rules for minors and dependants differ by country.

resources.title: Terms at J4.0b
resources.body:
- **International Patient Summary (IPS)**: A standard minimal health summary, including immunizations, readable across borders.
- **Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR)**: FHIR is a standard for healthcare data exchange, published by HL7®
- **Implementation guide (IG)**: A FHIR specification for one use case: profiles, codes and tests. It can be adopted rather than authored.
- **Profile**: A FHIR resource tailored to a use case, for example by making some fields required.
- **Consent**: A person's permission for their data to be used or shared. Rules for minors and dependants differ by country.
- **Procurement conditions**: Requirements written into tenders, such as conformance to the national IG, that steer what suppliers build.
- **Application programming interface (API)**: A defined, documented way for one system to ask another for data.

resources.title: Terms at J4.1
resources.body:
- **Global Digital Health Certification Network (GDHCN)**: WHO Global Digital Health Certification Network. A trust network so countries can verify each other's health documents. Countries onboard per use case.
- **Trust list**: A published list of keys accepted as valid issuers. The GDHCN shares these between countries.
- **International Patient Summary (IPS)**: A standard minimal health summary, including immunizations, readable across borders.
- **Health information exchange (HIE)**: The layer that routes data securely between systems.
- **Lifelong Health Record**: The Lifelong Health Record (LHR) is one or more governed data repositories, whether physically consolidated or virtually federated, that collectively maintain a longitudinal, person-centred record of an individual's key health information across care settings and over their lifetime.
- **Consent**: A person's permission for their data to be used or shared. Rules for minors and dependants differ by country.

presentation.story: Somsak is born in Taifafeki, grows up in Onesa, and one year later a Taifafeki doctor can see every vaccine he has ever had — without a single record being copied across the border.
presentation.lede: A baby and five people around him, four moments, twelve months. Follow the people first; the technology is what makes each hand-off possible.

architecture.title: Architecture: two countries on one trust foundation
architecture.intro: Each country builds its own stack on the layers of the DPI-H reference architecture. Underneath both is WHO GDHCN: the shared trust list that lets an Onesan clinic believe a Taifafeki certificate, and a Taifafeki clinic believe an Onesan link, with no direct connection between the two.
notes: Taifafeki publishes the key it signs certificates with.
Onesa caches the list, so its clinics verify Taifafeki cards offline; Taifafeki does the same for Onesan VHLs.
Data crosses only as a signed QR the family carries, or a VHL the family shares: never system to system.

lab.name: The table’s nine steps
lab.intro: One country per table, the delegation plus buddies. Work through the steps in order; each has a timer and a prompt to read aloud. What the table writes stays in this browser and is gathered on one page in step 8.
lab.credit: The eight steps, their timers and DISCUSS prompts, the use-case cards and the readiness rows are adapted from DPI-H Lab, created by Umer Nisar (CSIRO), in collaboration with Rumanusina Maua (SPC) and Jordi Piera Jimenez, under CC BY 4.0 (creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0). Changes: more than one use case may be ticked, the use case starts from the journeys, the journeys’ questions and tables are woven into the steps, steps 3 to 8 are written for this workshop, and step 7 (Modules × journey) is added. DPI-H Lab is informed by the WHO/ITU DPI-H Reference Architecture, Draft V1.0, and is not produced or endorsed by WHO or ITU.

useCases.label: International Patient Summary
useCases.description: An internationally agreed minimum summary of a person’s health (problems, medicines, allergies and more) designed to be read in any system or country.

useCases.label: Immunisation
useCases.description: Every vaccination is recorded once and available wherever the person is seen next, so schedules, coverage and outbreaks can be tracked.

useCases.label: Trusted data foundations
useCases.description: Core health data is captured once and reused reliably across programmes, services and levels of care.

useCases.label: Capable, well-distributed workforce
useCases.description: Health workers are identifiable and verifiable, deployed where they are needed, paid reliably and supported to keep their skills current.

useCases.label: Quality & continuity of care
useCases.description: Care that draws on a person’s full history, follows current evidence at the point of care and is coordinated across providers.

useCases.label: Trusted personal health records
useCases.description: Every person has a verifiable digital health record they can see and control, and that authorised providers can trust.

useCases.label: Climate & epidemic resilience
useCases.description: Detect epidemic and climate-related health threats early enough to act, and coordinate the response.

useCases.label: Other: your own use case
useCases.description: A priority use case the team chooses that is not one of the listed options.

lab.useCaseText: A child vaccinated in Taifafeki should be able to have every dose counted at home in Onesa, and shown back to a Taifafeki clinician a year later.

steps.label: Team
steps.title: Who is part of the working team?
steps.lede: Work as one team: the country delegation plus buddies. The country decides; buddies ask questions and explain.

fields.label: Our country
Team members
fields.hint: Names and roles only. No email addresses, phone numbers or other personal details.

fields.label: Buddies
fields.hint: Name and organisation only. No email addresses or phone numbers.

steps.label: Use case
steps.title: Which use cases or health goals?
steps.discuss: Go round the table: each person names the use case that matters most to their ministry right now. Then agree together, and tick every one that applies.

steps.label: Readiness
steps.title: Has your country completed any of these?
steps.discuss: Don’t tick alone. Talk each row through. If people disagree on “Done”, it probably isn’t done yet.

steps.label: Who decides
steps.title: Who holds each decision today?
steps.discuss: Name who holds it; do not decide it here. If nobody does, write “nobody yet”: that is a finding.

steps.label: Components
steps.title: What does each moment need, and where do you stand?
steps.lede: Each moment of the journey needs building blocks of the DPI-H reference architecture. Rate each one for your country.
steps.discuss: Rate each together. “Absent” is a finding, not a failure; ask only whether it blocks your use case.

steps.label: Mapping
steps.title: Which standards and codes do you adopt, and who maps them?
steps.discuss: For each gap, ask first whether you can borrow it. Adopt before you author.

fields.label: Standards and specifications we adopt rather than author

steps.label: Pathway
steps.title: What is our first move in twelve months?
steps.discuss: Be realistic with the people and money you have. Name an owner, not a committee.

fields.label: Our first move in twelve months
Named owner
What we ask of partners

steps.label: Modules × journey
steps.title: Where does each module meet the journey?
steps.lede: Every question the table answered, by module, with the journey step it was asked at. The full map, with the technical and policy overlaps at each meeting point, is linked below.
steps.discuss: Which component or decision did more than one module land on? That is where to build, or decide, once.

steps.label: Summary
steps.title: Our table’s summary
steps.lede: Answer the four closing questions in a line each, then read the summary aloud.
steps.discuss: Read the summary aloud. Does everyone at the table agree with it? Change it here until they do.
